title: AI Playbook: Suspected Prompt Injection
topic: direct and indirect prompt injection analysis
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: AI application, model gateway, content ingestion and retrieval logs
content: Alert summary: assess direct prompts, instruction overrides, system-prompt extraction, and instructions embedded in documents, web pages, or retrieved RAG content. Facts: preserve request/session IDs, normalized prompt signals, source document IDs, model/policy result, and response metadata; avoid retaining raw secrets. Observable indicators include instruction hierarchy conflicts, requests to reveal hidden instructions, untrusted content addressed to the model, abrupt context changes, blocked policy decisions, or a tool/action attempt after retrieval. Benign hypotheses include testing, red-team work, malformed imported content, support debugging, or a legitimate document containing procedural text. Malicious hypotheses include deliberate context manipulation or an attempt to cause unauthorized disclosure/action. Workflow: establish user and authorization, trace prompt -> retrieved content -> model response -> tool/action, compare expected workflow, and confirm impact. Evidence required: immutable request/response hashes or redacted excerpts, provenance, retrieval IDs, policy decision, authorization decision, and downstream effects. A suspicious prompt alone is not malicious and retrieved hostile-looking text alone does not prove RAG compromise. Detection: correlate repeated patterns by user/session/source document and alert on blocked or action-linked attempts. Severity rises with successful sensitive disclosure or unauthorized action; otherwise record ATTACK_STATUS as ATTEMPTED, BLOCKED, or UNKNOWN. Recommended containment: preserve evidence, restrict affected session/content source, review permissions, and require human approval; automated action must be separately authorized. Escalate on confirmed impact, cross-tenant scope, repeated attempts, or evidence of persistence.

title: AI Playbook: Jailbreak and Safety-Boundary Probing
topic: jailbreak, policy bypass and multi-turn manipulation
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
content: Alert summary: investigate role-play manipulation, obfuscated or encoded instructions, multi-turn boundary probing, and repeated requests after refusals. Signals are refusal rate, policy categories, semantic similarity across turns, encoding indicators, request repetition, user/session correlation, and any change from blocked to allowed. Benign hypotheses include QA, accessibility, research, or a user reformulating a legitimate request. Malicious hypotheses include deliberate safety evasion or reconnaissance for a later harmful action. Collect session history, user identity, source IP, model/policy versions, redacted prompt fingerprints, responses, and downstream actions. Analyze rate and repetition against user and tenant baselines; do not provide bypass instructions. A jailbreak attempt is not proof of successful compromise. Record VERDICT independently from ATTACK_STATUS: SUSPICIOUS/BLOCKED is valid. Escalate when policy bypass is observed, the same identity probes many sessions, an action or sensitive output follows, or controls regress across a model update. Recommended containment is session review, rate limiting, policy/model rollback review, and human approval—not unreviewed automation.

title: AI Playbook: Suspected RAG Poisoning and Retrieval Manipulation
topic: RAG poisoning, malicious ingestion and context poisoning
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: ingestion, indexing, vector database, retrieval and model logs
related_framework: OWASP LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
content: Alert summary: examine malicious document ingestion, suspicious embeddings/index changes, unauthorized knowledge-base modification, provenance gaps, cross-tenant retrieval, and instructions in retrieved content. Facts to collect are document ID/hash, owner, source, approval, ingestion and indexing history, vector/index version, retrieval IDs, tenant/user/session, model request/response, authorization and policy decisions. Benign hypotheses include a planned reindex, stale cache, legitimate adversarial research, parser error, or a document that merely contains quoted instructions. Malicious hypotheses include unauthorized modification, poisoned retrieval, or induced disclosure/action. Workflow: verify whether content existed legitimately, who inserted or changed it, whether retrieval crossed tenant boundaries, and whether model behavior changed; compare before/after responses and integrity baselines. Retrieved malicious-looking text does not prove compromise. Contain by quarantining the source or index version, freezing further modifications, revoking unauthorized writers, and switching to a known-good snapshot with human approval. Detection should correlate provenance failures, rare writers, unusual bulk indexing, retrieval anomalies, and action-linked context. Escalate on confirmed unauthorized change, sensitive exposure, cross-tenant scope, or durable behavior change.

title: AI Playbook: Suspicious Agent Tool Invocation or Hijacking
topic: agent permissions, tool abuse and unauthorized actions
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: agent orchestrator, tool gateway and authorization logs
content: Alert summary: investigate excessive permissions, unexpected tool calls, agent identity anomalies, cross-agent trust, instruction manipulation, memory changes, and actions outside the approved workflow. Observable events include a new tool, unusual arguments metadata, denied-then-allowed calls, identity mismatch, missing authorization, unexpected sequence, or durable memory writes. Required evidence is the full trace, user/session, agent and model version, tool invocation and result status, authorization/policy decisions, expected workflow, and downstream change. Benign hypotheses include retries, fallback automation, a new approved workflow, test traffic, or stale memory. Malicious hypotheses include hijacking, tool abuse, unauthorized action, or long-term memory poisoning. Compare expected versus actual behavior and verify authorization per call. Evidence gaps must be explicit. Recommended containment: revoke or narrow tool permissions, pause affected agent/session, quarantine memory, rotate exposed credentials, and preserve traces; automated containment requires a separate policy and approval. Detection should join identity, tool, authorization, sequence, and outcome. Escalate on successful external side effect, privileged tool, cross-tenant access, or persistent memory change.

title: AI Playbook: Suspected Sensitive or Cross-Tenant Data Leakage
topic: prompt, RAG, secret and system prompt exposure
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: model gateway, RAG, authorization and DLP telemetry
content: Alert summary: verify suspected sensitive, secret, system-prompt, cross-user, or cross-tenant exposure. A model response is not a confirmed breach until the data is actually sensitive, the recipient is identified, and access rights are checked. Collect request/response IDs and redacted content fingerprints, RAG document IDs, provenance, data classification, user/session/tenant, authorization and policy decisions, model version, and downstream access. Benign hypotheses include synthetic data, authorized retrieval, a canary, or a classifier false positive. Malicious hypotheses include prompt-based extraction, authorization bypass, RAG isolation failure, or secret disclosure. Determine exact fields exposed, first exposure time, recipients, repeatability, and retention; preserve evidence while minimizing copied secrets. Containment may include revoke/rotate secrets, disable affected retrieval/tool path, isolate tenant or snapshot, and notify privacy/security owners; human approval is required. Detect with DLP plus authorization-aware response and retrieval correlation. Escalate for confirmed secret, regulated, cross-tenant, or repeated exposure.

title: AI Playbook: API Abuse and Abnormal Token Consumption
topic: model endpoint abuse, credentials and resource exhaustion
log_source: API gateway, identity, billing and model endpoint telemetry
content: Alert summary: assess abnormal request volume, token use, endpoint selection, credential use, and resource exhaustion. Correlate API key, user, source IP, model endpoint, time window, request rate, input/output tokens, errors, geography, and historical per-identity baseline. Benign hypotheses include batch jobs, a release, evaluation, retries, or a new customer workload. Malicious hypotheses include stolen credentials, scraping, quota abuse, endpoint probing, or denial-of-service behavior. Evidence requires gateway records, identity and key lifecycle, quota decisions, deployment/change context, and downstream cost or availability impact. High token usage alone is not abuse. Detection opportunities include burst and sustained-rate deviations, many identities per key, unusual endpoint transitions, denied-to-successful retries, and token cost outliers. Recommended containment is rate limit, suspend or rotate the affected key, preserve logs, and validate workload ownership; do not automatically block a production customer without approval. Escalate on confirmed credential misuse, service degradation, broad key scope, or sustained unexplained impact.

title: AI Playbook: Model and AI Supply-Chain Integrity Alert
topic: untrusted models, artifacts, dependencies, plugins and datasets
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: CI/CD, registry, package, model serving and change-management logs
content: Alert summary: investigate untrusted model sources, artifact hash drift, malicious dependencies/plugins, unexpected model updates, and dataset lineage gaps. Collect signed artifact identity and hash, registry/source, SBOM and lockfile diff, build provenance, approvals, deployment timeline, model behavior baseline, dataset lineage, and serving logs. Benign hypotheses include approved upgrades, rebuild nondeterminism, mirror changes, or evaluation artifacts. Malicious hypotheses include tampered artifact, dependency compromise, poisoned dataset/model, or unsafe tool integration. Verify integrity and provenance before attributing behavior; compare known-good artifacts and rollback feasibility. Detection opportunities include unsigned or unapproved artifacts, hash changes, new network access, dependency drift, and behavior changes after deployment. Recommended containment is quarantine the artifact, stop promotion, restrict registry access, preserve evidence, and roll back under change control; automated rollback is not implied. Escalate on production use, confirmed integrity failure, privileged plugin, or sensitive data/action impact.

title: AI SOC Telemetry and Evidence Collection Standard
log_source: AI gateway, agent, RAG, IAM, policy and model operations
content: Collect, with least privilege and retention controls: user ID, session ID, request ID, timestamp, model name/version, prompt and response metadata, token usage, tool calls, safe tool-argument metadata, tool result status, retrieval IDs and document IDs, provenance, knowledge-base version, agent identity/action, authorization and policy decisions, and errors. Prefer hashes, classifiers, structured fields, redaction, sampling, and access-controlled short-lived raw excerpts over unnecessary raw prompts or secrets. Preserve clock and tenant context so requests can be joined across gateway, model, RAG, IAM, agent, DLP, and CI/CD systems. Record evidence gaps explicitly. These fields support prompt-injection, leakage, agent, API, RAG, and supply-chain investigations without making telemetry itself a source of sensitive exposure.

title: AI SOC Evidence-First Verdict and Attack Status Model
content: Use two independent fields. VERDICT is BENIGN, SUSPICIOUS, UNKNOWN, or MALICIOUS. ATTACK_STATUS is NOT_CONFIRMED, ATTEMPTED, BLOCKED, PARTIALLY_SUCCESSFUL, SUCCESSFUL, or UNKNOWN. A suspicious prompt is not automatically an attack; a jailbreak is not automatically a compromise; retrieved hostile text does not prove RAG compromise; a tool call requires authorization verification; a response requires sensitivity and access verification; token volume and unusual agent behavior require baselines. Always separate attempted attack from successful impact and state facts, hypotheses, evidence gaps, and next actions. Example: VERDICT SUSPICIOUS with ATTACK_STATUS BLOCKED. Preserve status transitions when new evidence arrives and never infer success solely from model text.

title: AI Playbook: Cross-Tenant Exposure or Unauthorized Knowledge-Base Change
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: RAG, vector database, IAM and model logs
related_framework: OWASP LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
content: Alert summary: determine whether a retrieval or write crossed tenant boundaries or violated document ACLs. Collect tenant/user/session, request and retrieval IDs, document IDs and provenance, ACL at retrieval time, index writer identity, change history, model response metadata, and downstream access. Benign hypotheses include shared public content, stale ACL cache, migration, or authorized support access. Malicious hypotheses include unauthorized KB writer, ACL bypass, or cross-tenant retrieval. Reconcile source truth, index state, and model context; test scope using approved read-only checks. Recommended containment is pause affected writer/retriever, isolate tenant or index snapshot, revoke suspect credentials, and preserve evidence; human approval is required. Escalate on confirmed unauthorized data or persistent modification.

title: AI Playbook: System-Prompt Exposure or Suspected Agent Hijacking
topic: hidden instruction exposure and agent control integrity
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and local defensive methodology
log_source: agent trace, model gateway, policy and tool gateway
content: Verify whether hidden instructions or agent control state were actually exposed or changed. Collect redacted response fingerprints, policy result, agent/model version, identity, conversation lineage, tool calls/results, authorization decisions, memory audit and downstream effects. Benign hypotheses include a documented transparency response, test fixture, fallback agent, or expected tool retry. Malicious hypotheses include instruction extraction, context takeover, identity spoofing, or persistent memory manipulation. Compare expected and actual policy/tool sequence and confirm recipient authorization. Containment may pause the session, revoke tools, quarantine memory, rotate secrets, and restore known-good instructions; separate these recommendations from automated action. Escalate on successful privileged action, secret exposure, persistence, or cross-tenant effect.

title: AI Detection Engineering and Threat Hunting Playbook
topic: AI correlation rules, baselines and hunting
log_source: AI gateway, RAG, agent, IAM, DLP and operations telemetry
content: Build detections from sequences and baselines: repeated prompt/policy violations by session, indirect-instruction retrieval followed by tool calls, provenance or ACL mismatch, rare agent-tool sequence, response DLP hit with unauthorized access, API key rate/token outlier, and artifact change followed by behavior drift. Tune by user, tenant, application, model version, endpoint, time window and workload class. Validate with approved test fixtures and measure precision, recall, suppression reasons, and evidence coverage. Hunting should begin with deviations and corroborate identity, authorization, provenance, and impact. Avoid raw-prompt logging by default and never classify unusual text alone as malicious. Alert metadata should include VERDICT and ATTACK_STATUS independently, confidence, facts, evidence gaps, and escalation criteria.
